statement.p: If \displaystyle L=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \ \ \frac {dx}{dt}=-2, \ \mbox{and } \frac {dy}{dt}=4, find \displaystyle\frac{dL}{dt} when x=8 and y=3.

solution.p: We rewrite L=(x^2+y^2)^\frac{1}{2} and then take the derivative of both sides with respect to t. \frac{dL}{dt}=\frac{1}{2}\left(x^2+y^2\right)^{\frac{-1}{2}}\left(2x \frac{dx}{dt}+2y\frac{dy}{dt}\right) Then we substitute what we know and solve for what we don't know. \frac{dL}{dt}=\frac{1}{2}\left(8^2+3^2\right)^{\frac{-1}{2}}\left(2\cdot8 \cdot -2+2\cdot3\cdot4\right)=-0.468164588784522.
